subject: Business Management
name: Business Management, Units 3 and 4
about: VCE, Managing and transforming a business
syllabus: VCE Business Management Study Design (from 2023), Units 3 and 4

points.title: Types of business
points.brief: Sole traders, partnerships, private and public listed companies, social enterprises and government business enterprises differ in owners, liability and aims.

points.title: Social enterprises
points.brief: A social enterprise trades to meet a social or environmental purpose, and puts most of its profit back into that purpose.

points.title: Government business enterprises
points.brief: A business owned by government that sells goods or services and aims to make a profit while serving the public, such as Australia Post.

points.title: Business objectives
points.brief: Objectives such as making a profit, increasing market share, improving efficiency, improving effectiveness, meeting a social need and meeting shareholder expectations.

points.title: Stakeholders and their interests
points.brief: Owners, managers, employees, customers, suppliers, the general community and others each want different things from a business, which can clash.

points.title: Management styles
points.brief: Styles run from autocratic, through persuasive, consultative and participative, to laissez-faire, giving staff more say at each step.

points.title: Choosing a management style
points.brief: The right style depends on the task, the time available, staff experience and the manager's preference.

points.title: Management skills
points.brief: Communicating, delegating, planning, leading, decision-making and interpersonal skills. Each style leans on some skills more than others.

points.title: Corporate culture
points.brief: Official culture is the values a business states. Real culture is how staff actually behave. Managers can shape it through rewards, symbols and their own example.

points.title: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
points.brief: Maslow said people move up five levels of needs, physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation, once the level below is met.

points.title: Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory
points.brief: Goals motivate when they have clarity, challenge, commitment, feedback and suitable task complexity.

points.title: Lawrence and Nohria's four drive theory
points.brief: People are driven to acquire, to bond, to learn and to defend. A workplace that meets all four motivates staff best.

points.title: Performance-related pay
points.brief: Paying bonuses, commissions or profit shares for results can lift effort, but may push staff to compete instead of cooperating.

points.title: Career advancement and training as motivation
points.brief: The chance to be promoted, and investment in training, show staff a future in the business and build their skills.

points.title: Support and sanction strategies
points.brief: Support strategies, such as counselling and flexible work, help staff through problems. Sanctions, such as warnings, use the threat of losing something.

points.title: Training options
points.brief: On-the-job training happens while working, such as shadowing a colleague. Off-the-job training happens elsewhere, such as a course. Each has pros and cons.

points.title: Performance management
points.brief: Setting goals and measuring staff against them, through management by objectives, appraisals, self-evaluation and observation.

points.title: Termination management
points.brief: Employees leave by retirement, redundancy, resignation or dismissal. Each brings duties for the business, such as notice and entitlements.

points.title: Entitlements and transition
points.brief: Departing staff are owed unpaid wages, leave and sometimes redundancy pay. Transition help, such as outplacement, eases the move.

points.title: Roles in workplace relations
points.brief: Employees, human resource managers, unions, employer associations and the Fair Work Commission all play a part in setting pay and conditions.

points.title: Awards and agreements
points.brief: An award sets minimum pay and conditions for an industry. An enterprise agreement is negotiated in one workplace and must leave staff better off overall.

points.title: Resolving workplace disputes
points.brief: Disputes are settled first through grievance procedures inside the business, then if needed through mediation or arbitration.

points.title: Operations in manufacturing and services
points.brief: Manufacturing makes tangible goods that can be stored. Services are intangible and often made and used at once, with the customer present.

points.title: Inputs, processes and outputs
points.brief: Operations turns inputs such as materials, labour and money into outputs, through processes that add value.

points.title: Efficiency and effectiveness
points.brief: Efficiency is making the most output from the fewest inputs. Effectiveness is how well a business meets its objectives.

points.title: Technology in operations
points.brief: Automated production lines, robotics, computer-aided design, artificial intelligence and online services can cut costs and errors.

points.title: Materials management
points.brief: Forecasting demand, the master production schedule, materials requirement planning and just-in-time all keep the right materials on hand without waste.

points.title: Quality strategies
points.brief: Quality control inspects output for faults, quality assurance checks the process against a standard, and total quality management involves everyone in improving.

points.title: Waste minimisation
points.brief: Reducing, reusing and recycling materials in production cuts costs and harm to the environment.

points.title: Lean management
points.brief: Lean management cuts any step that adds no value, using pull production, one-piece flow, takt time and zero defects.

points.title: Corporate social responsibility in operations
points.brief: Using sustainable materials, cutting emissions and treating suppliers fairly go beyond what the law asks.

points.title: Global considerations in operations
points.brief: Global sourcing of inputs and making goods overseas can lower costs but bring risks to quality, reputation and supply.

chapters.title: Reviewing performance and the need for change

points.title: Forms of business change
points.brief: Business change is any shift in how a business works. It can be proactive, made before problems arise, or reactive, made in response to them.

points.title: Performance indicators (KPIs)
points.brief: Measures of how a business is going, such as net profit, market share, productivity growth, sales, staff absenteeism and turnover, wastage, complaints and workplace accidents.

points.title: Lewin's force field analysis
points.brief: Lewin said change happens when the forces for it outweigh those against it. Managers weigh and rank the forces, act, then check the result.

points.title: Driving forces for change
points.brief: Owners, managers, employees, competitors, laws, profit, cutting costs, globalisation, technology, innovation and social attitudes can push a business to change.

points.title: Restraining forces against change
points.brief: Managers and employees who resist, lack of time, organisational inertia, laws and cost can hold change back.

points.title: Porter's generic strategies
points.brief: Porter said a business gains an edge by lower cost (cost leadership) or by being different in a way customers value (differentiation).

points.title: The importance of leadership in change
points.brief: Leaders set the direction of change, explain why it is needed and keep staff on board through it.

points.title: Management strategies to improve performance
points.brief: Staff training, staff motivation, a change of management style, redeploying resources, innovation, new technology, cost cutting and lean production.

points.title: Redeployment of resources
points.brief: Moving natural, labour and capital resources to where they add more value, such as shifting staff to growing parts of the business.

points.title: Developing corporate culture
points.brief: Managers can build a culture that welcomes change through shared values, rewards, stories and their own example.

points.title: Senge's learning organisation
points.brief: Senge described a business that learns and adapts, through systems thinking, personal mastery, mental models, building a shared vision and team learning.

points.title: Overcoming resistance with low-risk strategies
points.brief: Communication, empowerment, support and incentives help staff accept change and keep trust.

points.title: High-risk strategies against resistance
points.brief: Manipulation and threat may force change quickly, but can damage trust, morale and the business's reputation.

points.title: Lewin's three-step change model
points.brief: Unfreeze old ways, make the change, then refreeze so the new ways stick.

points.title: Effects of change on stakeholders
points.brief: Change affects managers, employees, customers, suppliers and the community in different ways, some good and some bad.

points.title: Corporate social responsibility in change
points.brief: Change should be carried out ethically, considering staff, the community and the environment, not only profit.

points.title: Reviewing performance indicators after change
points.brief: After change, managers check the same indicators again to see whether the strategy worked.
